analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from using plan amendments to whittle down older workers' already-earned pension benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the Senate health committee in September 1999 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2001, without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal pension law to stop a practice known as 'wearing away' of benefits. Under some pension plan amendments, a worker's accrued benefit — including early retirement subsidies — can end up worth less than what they had already earned, because the new formula cuts future accruals so sharply. The bill defined accrued benefits so that workers in plans with 100 or more participants could never see their earned benefit shrink below what they had accumulated under the old terms, applying to plan amendments taking effect after June 29, 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and over (the 'older workers' of the title) in medium and large companies with traditional defined benefit pensions. If an employer adopted an amendment cutting future accruals, these workers would keep the full benefit they had already earned, including early retirement subsidies, instead of watching it erode. Workers who are close to retirement have the most to lose from wear-away amendments and the most to gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older workers in traditional pension plans

how_it_helps.text: It amends ERISA so that, for defined benefit plans with 100 or more participants, a plan amendment is treated as reducing accrued benefits if the worker's benefit could at any point fall below what they earned before the amendment plus what the current formula gives for later years of service [S2] [S3].

The protection expressly covers early retirement benefits and retirement-type subsidies for workers who meet the plan's conditions, so employers could not use amendments to strip back those subsidies from employees near retirement [S3].
It applies to plan amendments taking effect after June 29, 1999, closing the door on pending as well as future wear-away amendments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor large defined benefit plans would give up the ability to reduce what older employees have already accrued through plan amendments — a flexibility that, when used, shifts pension costs onto the workers who earned the benefits. The compliance burden is modest: plans simply must not structure amendments in a way that wears away earned benefits.

drawbacks.text: The restriction applies only to plans with 100 or more participants, so workers at smaller companies get no protection from the same wear-away practice [S3].

Employers would argue the rule limits legitimate plan redesign; a company trying to modernize its pension formula for all future hires would face constraints on how the transition affects current older employees, and the federal rules governing pension amendments are already complex enough that adding another test raises compliance costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and real: it closes a specific gap in ERISA that lets a worker's earned pension shrink through the back door of a plan amendment, and it protects early-retirement subsidies that matter most to people just short of retirement age. The costs fall on plan sponsors as reduced flexibility and some compliance work, which is the point of the rule. The main design weakness is the 100-participant threshold, which leaves smaller-plan workers exposed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on September 16, 1999, joined by Sens. Leahy, Jeffords, Reid, Kennedy, and Wellstone as original cosponsors [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or House counterpart action — appears in the bill's history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with large defined benefit pension plans are better off: they kept the ability to reduce older employees' future accruals and early-retirement subsidies through plan amendments, which the bill would have prohibited. Workers near retirement in those plans gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Sen. Jim Jeffords, a Republican, was an original cosponsor and the bill's 9 cosponsors split 8 Democratic and 1 Republican — but no vote was ever recorded, so the chamber's partisan shape on the bill is unknown.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring large defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill would bar these employers from adopting amendments that reduce older workers' already-earned benefits and early-retirement subsidies — a cost-shifting tool it would eliminate. Workers in those plans keep what they earned.

industries.industry: Pension consultants and benefits law firms
industries.note: A new ERISA test for plan amendments would create compliance work for benefits advisers, but it is a minor effect compared with the main stake.
